analysis.one_liner: Lets federal agencies override drug and medical patents when prices are excessive or health needs go unmet.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to two House committees and their subcommittees, received no hearing or vote, and died when the 107th Congress ended in January 2003.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would let the Department of Health and Human Services and the Federal Trade Commission authorize competitors to make patented drugs, devices, and other health inventions without the patent holder's permission. They could do this when the patent holder charges excessive prices, blocks needed products, refuses reasonable research licenses, or fails to develop the invention. Brand-name drug makers would also have to file annual audited reports on their pricing and research costs, with fines for failing to report.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients and health payers, who would gain access to cheaper versions of patented medicines when agencies find pricing excessive or health needs unmet. Generic and biosimilar manufacturers would gain a lawful pathway to make those products. Researchers would gain access to patented inventions needed for public-health research.

how_it_helps.text: The bill lets HHS and the FTC license patented health inventions to others without the patent holder's consent when the holder prices the invention excessively, engages in anticompetitive behavior, fails to develop it, or refuses reasonable research licenses.
Patent holders would still be paid adequate remuneration, and regulators must weigh the need for innovation incentives alongside the public's interests as patients and payers.

Drug makers would have to file annual audited reports on pricing and research-and-development costs for patented drugs, giving Congress and regulators visibility into what patients actually pay versus what development costs.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name pharmaceutical and biotech companies, whose exclusive patent rights would become conditional: agencies could authorize competitors to make their products, and they would face annual pricing audits with civil penalties up to $25,000 per day for noncompliance.

drawbacks.text: Compulsory licensing weakens the reward that patents provide; the bill itself requires regulators to weigh 'the need for adequate incentives for the creation and commercialization of new inventions,' an acknowledgment that easier licensing could slow development of new medicines.

The 'excessive pricing' standard — judged against median prices in developed countries or other reasonable standards — gives agencies broad discretion over whether a drug's price is lawful, which industry would argue creates uncertainty that discourages investment.
Annual audited reporting of worldwide pricing and research costs would impose compliance costs on any company selling a patented drug.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core tradeoff is classic: cheaper medicines and more access now, versus possibly slower development of future drugs. The bill tries to soften this by requiring that patent holders be paid for use of their inventions and by listing innovation incentives as a factor regulators must consider. The cost falls on a specific, highly profitable industry; the benefit spreads across every patient and insurer that pays drug prices.

outcome.mechanism: The House sent the bill to the Judiciary and Energy and Commerce committees on the day it was introduced; the subcommittees that received it never acted, and the bill died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Sherrod Brown of Ohio introduced the bill on May 3, 2001, with 23 original cosponsors — 21 of 208 House Democrats, the chamber's lone Independent, and one of 223 House Republicans.
The House referred the bill to the Judiciary Committee and the Energy and Commerce Committee on the day of introduction.
Within two weeks, it was split between the Judiciary Subcommittee on Courts, the Internet, and Intellectual Property and the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health.
No further action was recorded for the rest of the 107th Congress, which ended January 3, 2003; the bill never received a hearing mark, a committee vote, or a floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name pharmaceutical companies are better off: their exclusive patent rights stayed fully intact, with no compulsory-licensing threat and no annual pricing audits.

sides.party_line_note: Support was almost entirely Democratic — 21 of 208 House Democrats plus the chamber's lone Independent — with just one of 223 House Republicans signing on, and no committee or floor action ever occurred.

industries.note: The bill would let regulators authorize competitors to make patented drugs when prices are judged excessive, and would require annual audited reporting of pricing and research costs. This directly threatens the monopoly pricing power that drives drug industry profits.

The compulsory-licensing power covers any health care product — drugs, devices, biologics, and health technology — not just medicines. Their patent exclusivity would become conditional, though they would still be owed remuneration for use of their inventions.
Compulsory licensing would create a lawful pathway to make copies of patented medicines when regulators find excessive pricing or unmet health needs, expanding their addressable market.
